chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Paul Robeson as a neighbor at Riverton
summary: In later years Collins got to know Robeson in the Riverton apartments and says he sacrificed his career to make white America reckon with Black people.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Did you ever get to know Paul Robeson at all on all those dates you played with him or --

Well, I didn't get to know him then, because I couldn't get to him for the people. But in later years he moved into my -- I lived in a -- let's see, how do I say it, the metropolitan development. It's like apartments -- it's called the Riverton in New York, 135th and Madison. And he also lived in this development. I got to know him then. Beautiful man, just a marvelous, marvelous human being. And I realized that this man sacrificed his whole career for --
We were talking about Paul Robeson.

Yeah, I realized in later years that this man sacrificed his whole career to make the white man aware of the Negro. Because Paul Robeson at this time was -- he was a brilliant actor, a brilliant singer, he was a Rhodes scholar, he was an all American football player, he was just everything. And he just killed himself, you know, his career. But in doing so he made the white man aware of the fact that he had to reckon with the black man. He just couldn't take him as Sambo, you know. He -- Jackie Robinson, I remember when he -- he didn't understand Paul Robeson at first. He -- but he finally came around and recognized the fact that Paul Robeson was a great man in what he had done for his people.
And I would catch him out in the court every now and then in Riverton and just talk to him, and it was just the man had a beautiful philosophy, he was a beautiful human being.
He was very, very interested in all kinds of music.
-- and he had done a lot of studying because he believed that in the possibility that some of the roots of jazz were -- roots of European music were African.
He found similarities in European clas-
-- American jazz, and I had think it's a fascinating -- conversation with him once,
